Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the fastest way to earn money?
Answer: Last weekend, I made $5000 in a little more than 20 minutes. Here’s a picture to prove it. No, I didn’t sell drugs. I didn’t become a pornstar. I didn’t even start a business. I competed in a martial arts tournament, and I won. That’s it. I had 3 matches. The first match lasted 8 minutes. The second match went for about 2 minutes, and the 3rd and final match went for 10 minutes. I was on the mat fighting for a little more than 20 minutes. I won all 3 matches, and I was awarded a $5000 prize for my efforts. $5000 in 20 minutes of work. An easy day at the office, right? Wrong. Very wrong. There wasn’t much about this weekend that was easy, but, it was very quick. I endured quite a bit of pain, for a moderate amount of time, and I was awarded money — only because I was successful. I did make $5000 in 20 minutes, but in reality, it took me about 12 years to develop the skills to even have a chance at winning this tournament on Saturday. I made $5000 in 20 minutes, but in the long run, when it comes to my Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu “career” (a word I didn’t feel comfortable even using until about 6 months ago), I’ve lost a lot of money over the last 7 years. That’s why I wanted to write this answer about long-term goals and short-term payoffs. It takes a ridiculous amount of time to do something at a high level. I am not the most talented athlete. I’m not the most talented at anything. I don’t have magic genetics that made me a high-level athlete from a young age. When I played baseball growing up, it took me 2 years to develop enough hand-eye coordination just to hit the fucking ball. I spent the first 2 years of my baseball career celebrating foul balls and “foul tips” because they were “contact”. Contact was my indication of progress. I tried out for my school’s basketball team in middle school when I realized that the baseball thing wasn’t really working out, and I didn’t get past the first cut in basketball. Unfortunately, being 4'11 and chubby doesn’t exactly help you get the coach’s attention at basketball tryouts. After that was when I started wrestling, and I didn’t exactly have any success on the wrestling mat at first either. In 8th grade (my second year of wrestling — you know, when I was supposed to be better than my first year), I finished with 4 wins and 28 losses (more than double the amount of losses of my first year). Most of the losses were from pins. I spent most of my first 2 years involved in combat sports getting thrown around the ring, getting pinned, and then crying in the bleachers while munching on the post-competition Snickers bar that my mom or dad bought me. The point is, I wasn’t a talented wrestler, either. By my senior year of high school, I was winning more matches than I was losing, but I wasn’t winning tournaments. I never qualified for the state tournament. I wasn’t good, and I got better, but I never became great. Once wrestling was done, I started Jiu-Jitsu. This was the first time I was able to excel at something, but my success has never been linear. It takes a ridiculously strong mind to do something at a high level. When I started Jiu-Jitsu, I didn’t have any success either. I came in with a wrestling background, and that meant that I was supposed to have instant success in Jiu-Jitsu, but I didn’t. Again, I was winning more than I was losing, but I wasn’t great at Jiu-Jitsu and I didn’t have great results in Jiu-Jitsu. I was solid, but solid does not mean great. My goal wasn’t to be “solid”. My goal was to be world-class. Finally, at around 19, I started to get my “man-body”. That helped. But muscles alone weren’t enough to help me achieve my goals. I also had to develop world-class technique, precise timing, and a mind that could do all these things under intense pressure. What shifted over the course of that ridiculously long amount of time that I spent competing in martial arts was that I developed the mind of a successful martial arts competitor. I did this by studying philosophy, writing about my anxiety, practicing good habits, and yes, training a metric fuck-ton of Jiu-Jitsu on top of that. Now that I’m doing fairly well in Jiu-Jitsu, a lot of people seem to assume that I’m this talented guy who has some abilities that other people don’t have or that I just have ridiculously good luck. Those people weren’t here 11 years ago when I looked like a “roly-poly” on the mat — my dad’s words. I’ve done what I do with an intense amount of focus for a very long time. That’s pretty much it. That’s more important than talent. That’s more important than hard work. That’s more important than anything if you ask me. It takes a village to do something at a high level. Okay, this answer has been all about me so far. It’s time to shift the focus. For a long time, I was really concerned with being “self-made”. I wanted everyone to know that I had worked my ass off for everything that I achieve. I wanted everyone to know that I did it all myself. The problem is, that wouldn’t be the truth. I didn’t do this all on my own. I had a lot of help. In the picture above, the guy on my left (Jack) has been traveling with me and competing with me for nearly the last 4 years, and the guy on my right (my coach, Jeff) has been teaching me most of the Jiu-Jitsu I know since I was 17-years-old. Those are just 2 of the people that make up this village of friends and teammates that I have that help me do the things that I do at a high level. I’m just a vessel or something. Apart from just my training partners at the gym, there are also the guys who I’ve met through training out of town who have pushed me to reach for goals that I previously couldn’t have fathomed, and there are also the countless strangers who have said nice (and not-so-nice) things to me on the internet for the last year and a half that I’ve been sharing my life through writing. Both the good and bad comments motivate me in different ways. If you clicked on this answer because you wanted to learn about how to make $5000 in 20 minutes, I apologize immediately. I can’t teach you fast and easy ways to succeed. I can, however, show you that quick success does not exist. None of the things that I do well come easy to me. I could never win any grappling tournaments without training and working my butt off. I could never write good writing without editing it an obnoxious amount of times. I could never make good decisions without making stupid ones first. Maybe you’re the same way. Maybe my “advice” is useless, and maybe you’re going to go into your life and do the opposite of what I say. If that’s you, I respect it. I’ve been that guy. However, those readers are not the reason I write. I write for the people who can and are willing to learn for me. First and foremost, the person who can learn the most from the dumb shit I’ve done is myself. Here’s to not making the same mistakes over and over again.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the best way to make money?
Answer: Making money is harder when it comes from something you love. I’ve been doing Jiu-Jitsu for about 7 years, competing for more than 6 years, and competing at the “world level” for about 5 years. I didn’t start making enough money to live as an athlete until this year—2022. Originally, I thought that money didn’t exist in Jiu-Jitsu. Jiu-Jitsu, as I understood it, was an amateur sport. Then, I realized something. I didn’t realize it on my own, either. I realized it because of a friend who was a few steps above me in his career. He had a much more professional approach than I did. Jiu-Jitsu was an amateur sport for me because I was competing in amateur events. I wasn’t getting paid because I was taking every opportunity to compete possible. I didn’t really care if there was money on the line, a gold medal, or just some social clout. I loved Jiu-Jitsu, so I just fought because I loved it. I wasn’t a professional though. Looking back, this approach had some great benefits (I got a lot of experience, became good at competing, and became good at handling competition nerves), but it also had some drawbacks too. I got injured a lot, didn’t make money most of the time, and I spent a lot of my own money and time traveling to events, training myself, and working weird jobs to pay for competitions and travel. What a lot of people don’t realize is that most of the medal pictures I post on here won me zero dollars. I used medals as a way of building my teaching pedigree, but I didn’t get paid directly from competition until earlier this year. The only thing that changed was my mindset. I stopped viewing myself as “a grinder” and started viewing myself as a racehorse. I started viewing myself as a prizefighter. If that sounds pretentious to you, don’t worry. I didn’t like it at first either. In sports, it’s not smarter to fight every weekend. UFC fighters fight 3–4 times per year, and that’s a very active year. Jiu-Jitsu is less taxing than MMA, so I figured I could compete every couple of weeks without a problem. I had a meeting with a strength coach, and when I told him about my competition schedule, he basically laughed at me for thinking it was possible to be at my best every weekend without consequences. He told me about a bodybuilder who was hustling like a lunatic, trying to maintain peak performance every weekend, and using small shows (where he was paid $500 or less) to make his living. After about 6 months, he died. So what’s the point? The point is that you can’t nickel and dime your way to big success. You need to take stepping stones, but if you never take big shots, you’ll never get the big wins. I ain’t rich, but I’m also not fighting for free anymore. I make several times what I did last year and I’m doing the same things. The best way to make money is to know your worth and not accept anything less that what you are worth. If you can do this, you will get ahead of most people. Oh, but there’s a caveat. If you think you’re worth $1000 per hour, you better work like someone who’s worth $1000 an hour. You better deliver at least $1000 per hour worth of benefit to your customers. Skill pays. If you want to make money, do whatever it is you do really fucking well.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Is martial arts a lifestyle?
Answer: I could have had a very normal life. My parents live relatively “normal lives”. My non martial arts friends live pretty normal lives. I had a mostly normal childhood (although, probably a bit more exposure to mental illness than the average person). Doing the normal stuff—getting a regular job, going to normal social gatherings with friends, or other normal people things (like going to the movies or the mall or whatever)—was definitely an option for me. That was going to be, until the first day I walked into a Jiu-Jitsu academy. I know it sometimes sounds like that I’m bragging when I say that I “gave up a normal life for this”, but that’s not my intention. Really, I’m just trying to understand the bizarre reality that I’ve created myself. I literally fight crazy people for money. This is my job right now. Sorry if I think it’s weird. The other thing that I think that is really important to understand that the average martial artist doesn’t go through their life the same way I do. For me, martial arts is a lifestyle because it’s literally my entire life. Jiu-Jitsu is my favorite sport, my passion, and my job. For other people, martial arts is their hobby. This means that it might be part of their lifestyle, but that doesn’t mean that their whole lifestyle is martial arts-related. The beauty of martial arts is that you get out what you put in. If you want new friends, personal development, or maybe even a job, you can get that from martial arts by investing hours upon hours of your time. If you just want to get in better shape, you get that too. It’s up to you.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do people write such lengthy answers on Quora?
Answer: I started writing on Quora because in July of 2021, I read Nicolas Cole’s book, The Art and Business of Online Writing. (This is not an ad for that book btw. I don’t know Mr. Cole and apart from the $9.80 I spent on buying his book, I never have given him any of my money. The book was just a great way to learn about different places to write on the internet) That book was literally the whole reason I revisited Quora after years of barely scrolling through the site. I had created a Quora account years before, but I was too anxious to publish anything and I naively thought that writing on Quora “wouldn’t be worth it”. The reason that I decided to write on Quora in the first place was because I thought it would help me get better at writing while putting myself in front of a new audience (I started writing on Medium 10 months before I posted my first Quora answer). So yes. I started writing on Quora beacuse I wanted to advance my career. That was basically the only reason. I didn’t start writing on Quora because I’m some saint who just wants to help people. I didn’t start writing on Quora because I thought it would make me money. I started writing on Quora because I thought it would help me improve my skills to the point where I could maybe make money in the future. And? I was sort of right, but it took a while. Along the way, I’ve come to love Quora for what it really is: the Wild West of Digital Writing. Quora is not a traditional “Question and Answer” site. This isn’t a site for learning basic information. It’s not a site where you’re going to learn who the 23rd president of the United States was (although, for the sake of contradicting myself, it was Benjamin Harrison). This is a storytelling website. My first 89 Quora answers got around 6000 views cumulative (and not even 30 upvotes), and my 90th answer had several hundred thousand views and nearly 1000 upvotes in just a few days. I didn’t know much about Quora at the time, and I didn’t know much about the value that you could have on a community from a single answer, but my first “viral” answer taught me a lot about what Quora is all about. I’ve gone viral on Quora a bunch of times. One of my answers has more than 2 million views. I’ve realized however, that Quora isn’t about “going viral”. It’s not about answering questions, and it’s not even about “providing value”. The point of Quora goes deeper than whatever it is you have to say. The premise of Quora isn’t “this is what I know”. The premise of Quora is “this is what happened to me, and here’s what I learned”. Each frequently visited question has dozens (oftentimes more) replies and answers, and if you read through all of these answers, you’ll read the perspectives and stories of dozens of different individuals. Individuals. People. You’ll get a bunch of different worldviews, just from clicking on one question. If you click on “How can I overcome the fear of failure?”, you’ll see my essay on middle school wrestling. You’ll see James Altucher’s story of when he quit his job. You’ll some lady’s story of how she became a doctor. You’ll see a lot of really cool stories. The reason that people write long answers here on Quora is not to be pretentious, it’s because they’ve got stories to tell. That’s it, and that’s what I love about Quora. There are barely any rules here, barely any regular people, and a lot of people with freaking awesome stories. It’s the Wild West of Digital Writing., and I think that’s badass.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Who are you beyond Quora?
Answer: Here's me, beyond Quora. When I'm not writing, I'm probably either doing Jiu-Jitsu, eating, or sleeping. I train Jiu-Jitsu 2-3 times per day, 6-7 days per week. As I've gotten older and more banged up (this sport isn't exactly great for the ole body), I've begun to vary the intensity of these training sessions, but I'm still in the gym every day multiple times per day. I also teach private lessons and seminars all over the place. That's me off Quora in a nutshell. On Quora, I feel like I'm the "martial arts self-help/life lessons dude", but that's not always who I am in real life. In real life, I'm a 24-year-old (almost 25!) Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu athlete and teacher. I'm also a writer and a ghostwriter. I've been doing Jiu-Jitsu for 7 years, and writing on the internet for nearly 2 years (November 2022 my writing career turns 2 😎). In Jiu-Jitsu, I'm currently the #13 ranked 170-pound competitor in the world (yeah, the whole world, and yeah, I feel like an imposter about it 😂). The photo above is from a pro tournament I did yesterday in Los Angeles, California, where I lost in the finals to the #10 ranked guy in the world in the final seconds. It hurt. Literally and figuratively. It was also awesome. Competing sends my emotions into overdrive. Sometimes, the pre-match feelings make me want to just give up because I'm so anxious. Sometimes, the adrenaline makes me physically stronger than I ever thought was possible. Sometimes, the wins make me so happy I cry. Same with the losses. Beyond Quora, I'm entrenched in this crazy world of fighting, constant hard training, and a deep study of trying to master one of the most complex sports in the world - submission grappling. What I love about Jiu-Jitsu is the mental challenge it gives me. I'm almost never the most athletic or explosive athlete in my division, so I'm forced to use my intellect to try to work my way toward submitting and defeating my opponents. Sometimes, I win. Sometimes, I don't. Either way, I put the same passion into Jiu-Jitsu that I put into all of my Quora answers, Medium articles, ebooks, and Substack posts. You might think it’s corny, but I don’t care. I love this shit. Beyond Quora, I'm just as passionate as I am off Quora, although probably a bit quieter. Beyond Quora, I'm an introvert. Anyway, back to fighting. I literally put my blood, sweat, and tears into martial arts, because that's the only thing I know how to do. I've been involved in combat sports since I was 12. Even though I'm a young man now, all I know how to do is to fight with the determination of a depressed chubby kid with something to prove. I try to have the same passion in my writing, although writing hasn't actually made me bleed yet. Here's to hoping it stays that way. 😅 If you want to read more about my life beyond Quora, the best thing you can do is check out my newsletter at the link below 😊

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I forget someone whom I once loved deeply?
Answer: This question reminds me of my ex-girlfriend who I thought was the love of my life. She told me I was the love of her life, and I believed her. And yet, here we are. Sometimes, I wish I could forget her. If there's anything I learned from the movie in the picture above (Eternal Sunshine of a Spotless Mind), it’s that you're not supposed to forget the people you once loved, even if it hurts to not forget them. You’re supposed to learn from them. This sounds nice in a self-help-esque Quora answer, but it’s really hard to do in reality. My ex who I broke up with last year was the first woman who I really loved. It was the first time I really loved a person who isn’t my mom, my dad, or my sister. I know I really loved her because still, after everything we went through, I can’t hate her or even be mad at her. I know I loved her because I kept trying to convince myself that I wasn’t in love. This love was a neurochemical hijacking in a way I had never experienced before, and though the breakup was more than a year ago now, I still miss her a lot. I’ve dated other people since her, but I still miss her. “There are plenty of fish in the sea”, but I miss her. I would take her back right now, even though doing it would be a horrible decision. Even though taking her back would destroy my mental health, drain the life out of me, and break me down, I know that if she showed up at my doorstep I couldn’t resist her. I think that’s love. I’m only 24 and I don’t know that much, but I don’t think love is always rational. I loved this girl so damn much, and I’ll probably never see her again. I probably shouldn't ever see her again. She was sweet and sensitive, yet strong and determined. She had the duality and complexity that I’ve always craved in a partner, and I miss that so much. But she also had this dark side that terrified me. She changed a lot in the time we were together, and eventually, we grew apart. We grew apart, but that doesn’t mean I lost the memories. For a long time, I wanted the “spotless mind”, just like in the movie. I still remember when she held me one December afternoon in Milwaukee and made me feel like I didn’t have to fight my way through every moment of my life anymore. I still remember when we would sit together on Saturday afternoons after Jiu-Jitsu training and read together. I still remember when we went on drives and talked about Nietzsche, Buddha, and Viktor Frankl. I still miss that stuff, but it’s gone now. Anyway—sorry for my sob story. The point I’m trying to make is that sometimes I wish I could just rip these memories out of my head so that I didn’t have to miss this girl who probably doesn’t even think about me anymore. That’s probably the part that hurts the most. I’m sure she’s moved on. I moved on too, but sometimes it doesn’t feel that way. This past breakup forced me to change the way that I approach moving on. In the past, I’d breakup with someone and drown myself in work and training to forget them, just long enough until I stumbled upon the next girl who I could go through the same toxic cycles with. This past breakup cut me so deep that I had to actually grow. I couldn’t lie anymore. I had to forgive her for hurting me. I had to forgive myself for not being good enough and not knowing enough. I had to forgive all parties involved, but I never forgot any of what happened. The ending hurt so bad that I had no choice but to carefully analyze each mistake each of made so that I could ensure that it wouldn’t happen again. I couldn't sleep for weeks after it happened, so I had all kinds of time. This past breakup changed the way that I view every single person I interact with. It made me more careful, more mature (I think), and more protective of my own peace and wellbeing. I won’t throw myself at anyone without a bloody care ever again. I don’t want to forget these valuable lessons. I don’t want this girl’s memory to haunt me forever, but I don’t want to forget the moments that made me feel so happy and in love. After the breakup, I found myself desperately chasing women in an effort to replace the feelings that I had when I was in love, but no one could satiate my rabid insecure child the way she did. This empty feeling meant to me at the time that I needed to get her back, so I tried to do that. Long story short, it didn’t work. In time (time is the best breakup medicine), I realized that with practice, I could love myself the way my first love loved me. I realized that I wasn’t even really looking for a girlfriend or a partner, I was looking for validation and protection. It didn’t even take a therapist for me to figure why that was something I felt was lacking. With practice, writing, mindfulness, and most importantly genuine self-sufficiency (which I didn’t have during my last relationship), I was able to patch up the hole in my heart pretty well. Hopefully, with more time, I’ll be able to truly open my heart again. Until then, I’m gonna focus on writing and pajama fighting.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I live a good life of travels and tourism?
Answer: I’ve been on 21 trips this year. It’s not all it’s cracked up to be. This photo is from Burano, Italy, where I spent a day a few weeks ago with my girlfriend. It’s a beautiful, small town just outside of Venice. We had to take a boat taxi to get there. How did I get to live a life of travel and (relatively frequent) tourism? Well, it was pretty simple. You can probably do it too. First, I was a brat who decided that he didn’t want to work “a real job”. When I was younger, I worked normal young person jobs, but there’s a gap on my resume from the time I was 22 onward. I worked in a restaurant when I was younger. I was a camp counselor. The reason? I became a “professional Jiu-Jitsu athlete” and “internet writer” instead. I gave up the stability to teach kids Jiu-Jitsu, private lessons (through word-of-mouth marketing alone), and create an online content portfolio. For a few years, my parents thought I was out of my f*cking mind. I lived in a shitty studio apartment where my rent was incredibly cheap — although, when I moved in, I couldn’t even afford it. A story for another day. On the side, I wrote copy for small businesses. I hustled like a maniac. My personal development routine bordered on insane. I woke up at 6am every day and either wrote or worked out. I wrote and trained Jiu-Jitsu all day long. I didn’t have any money, so I just threw myself into my crafts — writing, competing in Jiu-Jitsu, and teaching. It was stupid. I wouldn’t recommend anyone live like this. I was unstable because I was financially unstable. I did not socialize. I had no friends (except my friends from Jiu-Jitsu). I trained so hard that my body broke and I wrote so much that I had wrist injuries. When this happened, I kept working and training. I was determined to do “something” for myself. In the end (long story short), the hard work paid off, and I was gifted the opportunity to travel full-time for about 6 months. During this time, I had pretty much every experience you can imagine. I had my heart broken. I fell in love. I failed and spent thousands of dollars on investments that I still haven’t seen a dime of return from. I achieved some major goals, like placing in one of the biggest martial arts tournaments in Europe (despite going up in weight and being injured). I also had some really fun travel experiences, like spending a week in Italy with my girlfriend, walking the sunny beaches of San Diego, road-tripping across America and listening to one of my favorite novels, or crossing the border south and seeing Mexico for the first time. I’ve gotten to do the whole “travel the world” thing like my old hero, Anthony Bourdain, and I didn’t have to inherit a bunch of money, have rich parents, or even get a high-paying job. I nickeled and dimed my way all the way across the world, a handful of times. I traveled the world while being an online writer and competing in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu — a grappling art that you probably have never heard of. That’s pretty cool to me. But that’s not the end of the story, unfortunately. Or, fortunately, depending on how you look at it. When I was younger, I wanted my life to look just like the movies. I wanted to fall in love in Venice (I did), I wanted to work on my first book on a rainy day from a cafe in London, and I wanted to sip coffee with an eager grin while overlooking the Rocky Mountains. I wanted all these idyllic, movie-esque experiences, and I got them because I sought them. But they did not make me happy. They did not heal the wounds in my heart put there by past torments. Travel did not make me a happy person. You don’t need happiness or the novelty of travel to be complete, you need meaning. The problem is that a lot of us are so disconnected from meaning in our daily lives that the only place that we truly find it is through travel. When I was traveling the world, you know what I longed for? To be somewhere like where I am now, relaxing after a hard workout, writing something that interests me, and sipping a hot coffee while my beautiful girlfriend reads in the other room (she took this picture). Home is here. Travel is fun and can offer some fun experiences, but home is here.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Should I learn judo or jiu jitsu?
Answer: If you’re 6 and want to try and make it to the Olympics in 12 years, Judo. If you’re trying to learn how to actually fight someone, do Jiu-Jitsu. If you want to make money in martial arts, do Jiu-Jitsu. If you want to be a part of one of the fastest-growing martial arts in the world (behind probably only MMA), do Jiu-Jitsu. Judo focuses on throws and upper body attacks. In Judo, there’s also an aspect of the training called “newaza”, which translates to ground techniques. That’s basically Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Essentially, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu is newaza on steroids. This is because “newaza” is very limited. It ignores many aspects of grappling. I submitted a Judo Junior Olympian when I was just a purple belt in Jiu-Jitsu. He was quite upset about it. Leg locks are also illegal in judo. On the flipside, they are a centerpiece of learning modern Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. “Why would you ignore 50% of the human body?” is a cliche quote in BJJ at this point from BJJ legend Dean Lister (to John Danaher, who made the quote famous). Just about all Judo that I’m familiar with is done in the gi (I think there’s some no-gi Judo, it’s just uncommon). In Jiu-Jitsu, the average practitioner will practice both gi and no-gi every week. Modern Jiu-Jitsu is becoming a blend of Judo, freestyle and Greco Roman wrestling, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, sambo, and even American catch wrestling. It’s becoming really cool to watch and participate in. The other thing I like about BJJ is that the culture is very modern. BJJ is always evolving and it’s evolving very quickly. There’s no “old school martial arts bullshit”. I’m an adult. I don’t need some dude who I call “sifu” or “sensei” who tells me what moves I’m allowed to do and what is off-limits. I don’t need anyone telling me who I can’t train with and learn from. I train with friends from other academies all the time. I fly all over the world to train with people. I watch moves on Instagram and try to learn them. That’s how technical evolution happens in the modern world. Plus, now, there are even professional Jiu-Jitsu events all over the place to study and learn from. This weekend, I’m competing in one in California for $5000. Not a horrible prize for an emerging professional sport. When I was a white belt in 2015, there were only a handful of professional Jiu-Jitsu promotions in the world. Now, there are dozens. Some events are paying up to $100,000 in cash prizes. I’ve never seen this in Judo. This actually goes back to the point I made in the opening sentence. In part because there is no BJJ in the Olympics, the sport of Jiu-Jitsu is exploding. BJJ is entirely private. The early days of BJJ were financed by rich dudes who just wanted to see the art grow. The Olympics or any other large government body isn’t holding back the development of the sport, so it’s growing like crazy. People in Jiu-Jitsu don’t care about bureaucratic bullshit. People in Jiu-Jitsu do Jiu-Jitsu to escape that shit. In wrestling and judo, it’s also really hard to make money. Owning a judo school typically isn’t a super profitable business (how many working professionals want to get thrown on their heads after work?), and private wrestling schools are few and far between. There is also no money available for professional athletes in these sports. A top-of-the-line Jiu-Jitsu academy on the other hand can make 6 figures (or even more). Jiu-Jitsu as a community has also strived to create a culture that is accessible and appealing to the average person. As a result of this exploding culture, you’re seeing more and more professional Jiu-Jitsu athletes. The level of the sport is rising year after year. This year’s ADCC World Championship (Abu Dhabi Combat Club) in Las Vegas is going to be insane. You, the person reading this, can head down to your local BJJ academy tomorrow and take your first introduction class. Depending on where you go, you can probably take it for free. Jiu-Jitsu people just want you to join the culture. If the culture grows, we all live easier, get better, and learn more. That’s what Jiu-Jitsu is really about and that’s why I like it more than any other martial art.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: If you were to teach the world one thing, what would it be?
Answer: I guess what I really want to be able to teach people how to do is how to do difficult things. Here’s a little story from one of my Jiu-Jitsu classes about how I try to help my students learn how to tackle challenges. When I joined my school’s wrestling team in middle school, my coach used to say that anyone who could walk on their hands all the down to the end of the mat would be a state champion. I could never do it. I could hardly walk more than a few steps. I was never a good hand-walker. I was also never a state champion. I was average in all things combat sports for the entirety of my youth. I didn’t win anything that mattered until I was 22. By that time, I had been involved in combat sports for more than a decade and I was doing it for the love of it. By the time I had any real success on the mat, I was already intrinsically motivated, and that gave me the work ethic to develop the skill required to have competitive success. As a side project, I still never gave up on my hand-walking, either. By the time I could walk to the end of the mat on my hands, I was already a Jiu-Jitsu world champion, and I was walking on my hands for the hell of it. I’ve realized that my wrestling lessons have helped me develop intrinsic motivation from a pretty young age, and as a coach, I try to help people do the same things. I realized this more as a coach than an athlete, but it is true in whatever you do: intrinsic motivation is the key to achieving difficult goals over extended periods of time. This is how you can teach people to develop intrinsic motivation. If you can do x, you can (maybe) do y. One thing that I hear a lot in the writing world is something along the lines of “if you write every day for 10 years, you will be a 6-figure writer”. Unfortunately, the way the market works, this is not necessarily true. You might not attain any success in writing. Nothing is guaranteed. If you write every day, that doesn’t mean that you will be the next Stephen King or Mark Manson. However, I can guarantee that if you don’t practice writing just about every day, you will definitely not achieve any success in writing. The same is true for music. The same is true for Jiu-Jitsu. In order to develop the ability to do the work required to do something incredibly well, you have to do the thing not because you want to be good, but because you love doing the thing. You must drop the results-driven approach, and seek “flow”. This is what I taught a 6-year-old how to do over the last few months. If a child can learn to flow, so can you. My work life is split about 50% between writing and teaching/competing in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Most of my teaching income comes through private lessons and teaching classes at a local academy here in Chicago, where I teach kid’s Jiu-Jitsu classes 3 days per week. I’ve done this for 6 months now, and when I first started, I had the kids “walk on their hands” for one of their warm-up exercises. As a joke, I channeled my wrestling coach told them that if they could walk all the way down to the end of the mat on their hands without falling, they’d be world champions. When we started doing “handstand walks” during class, none of them could make it more than a few feet. Most of them still can’t. Most of them are not physically developed enough yet to walk on their hands. However, some of them love walking on their hands. For a few of my students, the difficult task of walking on your hands as far as you can is their favorite part of Jiu-Jitsu class. One kid who loves this a lot is Armani. “Coach, can we walk on our hands today?” Every single day that Armani is in class, he runs over to me during warm-ups and asks me if we can walk on our hands. Every. Single. Day. The only question I get asked more than “Coach, can we play dodgeball?” is “Coach, can we walk on our hands?”. Kids are funny like that. They’re consistent. Armani is undeniably consistent. When he started walking on his hands, he couldn’t get more than a few steps. After a few months of watching me walk on my hands, getting some pointers, and practicing at home on his own, Armani was able to walk almost all the way down the mat. That was when I decided to make a friendly competition out of our daily hand-walking exercise. “Whoever is the first person to walk all the way down the mat on their hands will get a candy bar of their choice from me,” I said one day a few weeks back. After I said this, a funny thing happened. Intrinsic motivation is the key to perfection. Once I presented the students with the option to win a candy bar, some of them started to practice hand-walking before and after class. They desperately wanted that free candy. Who wouldn't? To answer my own question — Armani wouldn’t. Armani didn’t. For Armani, this extrinsic motivation did very little for him because he was already intrinsically motivated. A few classes later, Armani successfully walked all the way down to the end of the mat on his hands without a problem. After he did this, I pulled him aside. “What kind of candy bar do you want? You won.” “What do you mean?” he replied. He had completely forgotten about the challenge. He was walking on his hands every day not because he wanted to win, not because he wanted a candy bar from Coach, but because he just liked walking on his hands. He won himself a free Milky Way bar that didn’t even really need. He earned it through hard work, dedication, and most importantly, enjoying the activity that he was doing. That last point is the most important. In closing… The most important aspect of learning to do difficult things is not being gritty, being tough, or even being resilient. The most important aspect of learning to develop a high level of skills over an extended period of time is learning to enjoy the difficult skill. This is why I’m very grateful that I started wrestling when I was just 12. Legendary wrestler Dan Gable once said, “once you’ve wrestled, everything else in life is easy”. Obviously, this isn’t really true, but there is some truth to it. Becoming a successful writer, grappler, business owner, or anything is still difficult when you have wrestling experience. However, what wrestling and other physical endeavors inadvertently teach you is to love the grind for the grind itself. There were moments during my career when I was completely miserable and the thought of dying was literally more appealing than stepping onto the mat. However, now, when I look back at my wrestling days, I can’t help but reminisce about the early morning bus rides in the freezing Chicago winter, the ridiculously hard workouts at all hours of the day, and the constant soreness and hunger that I felt when wrestling was my entire life. I sense that little Armani is going to feel a similar type of way about walking on his hands one day. He’s going to think it’s hard, he’s going think it’s frustrating, but he’s also going to think it’s an incredibly fun activity to do. Learning to love doing difficult things for no other reason than the fact that they’re fun is the key to doing difficult things easily.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is some good advice and tips for traveling alone?
Answer: Traveling alone is hard. I did the math today, and I’ve been on 19 trips this year for Jiu-Jitsu competitions, seminars, and training trips. I’m in San Diego right now, for the third time since June. The city is starting to feel familiar. I can get around parts of it without using my maps app. This trip is a little different than the last time I was here though, because I’m traveling by myself. It’s cool to get in a new place and do my favorite thing—I’m here to train and film an instructional DVD for my Jiu-Jitsu—but it’s a little lonely when I’m not at the gym. Last week I was in Toledo, Ohio, for training. It was fun to train and I definitely got better, but I missed my friends. The other night, I drove home to Chicago, and then the next morning I hopped on a plane and flew out here to SD. Loneliness in the road can be difficult to tame. I chose this life, I’m just a little lonely sometimes lately. Part of me longs for somewhere that feels like home. I’ve been on the road so much this year I don’t really remember what home feels like. One tip that’s helped me mentally when I travel alone has been learning to address my emotional needs by myself. If I’m lonely, I find someone to talk to. This is essential for me. If there’s no one to talk to (the 2 people I’m friends with in San Diego were busy today), I find some work to distract myself. I’ve been working a lot lately—-writing, training, teaching, etc. I’m not posting as many original Quora answers lately in part because I’m kind of sick of getting yelled at by people every time I open this app, but also because I’m focusing a bit more on the writing that is going to help me grow my career a bit. I’m trying to next the step, and I feel I’m getting closer. That’s why I keep traveling. I’m focusing on the mission. The mission requires travel, even when the beauty of travel is gone. Another tip for traveling alone is to remember why you’re traveling. Don’t forget what you want. If you haven’t figured out what you want, stop acting as if traveling to a new place is going to give you peace. Sorry that this answer became a diary entry. Hope this helps at least a bit. 😅

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do most people waste their life?
Answer: I don’t think most people waste their lives. (The glass is root beer. Hehe.) “Most people waste their lives” seems a bit harsh. I think that most people do end up dying with unfulfilled dreams, incomplete bucket lists, and regrets, but I don’t think that means these people are “wasting their life”. Wasting your life, to me is what happens when you don’t make an effort to live it. It’s not that hard to not waste your life. You just need to try to do your best with what you have. You just need to avoid sabotaging yourself. It’s easier said than done, but it’s really worth it. Just because you don’t realize all your dreams doesn’t mean your life is a waste. People who live unremarkable lives have plenty of people who love them, things they like to do, and goals they aspire to. This alone is, to me, enough to make a life worth living. Just because not everyone wants to be a billionaire, a celebrity, or even have the same life you do does not mean that their life is “a waste”.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How should a young person invest money?
Answer: Here are the best investments of time and money I’ve made before I turned 25: Actual investments I’m not an accountant, so I won’t tell you where to invest your money. My dad worked in the stock market for decades and he told me to invest $100 per month to get started. If you save $100 per month for 40 years, you’ll have almost $50,000. If you invest that money, you will have about $1 million. At the very least, investing just makes you feel like you’re being smart with your money. Writing online for a year. When I downloaded Medium, I was hesitant about paying the monthly $5. It’s the best investment I’ve made in my career. I’ve made thousands in return and it’s only been 2 years. I have hundreds of email subscribers, average tens of thousands of monthly views on Medium, and I get about 1 million views per month on Quora (for now I guess, haven’t been writing here very much lately). I’m not saying that to brag. I’m saying that because it’s shocking to me that so many people would ever view my words. That’s the beauty of writing online. The best way to improve your thinking and the quality of your ideas is to publish them in written form. Give it a year. It takes at least 6 months for anyone to notice you—sometimes more. After that, you’ll probably get addicted. Training Jiu-Jitsu I’ve spent a lot of money on Jiu-Jitsu training, traveling to train, and competing. I saw no financial ROI before this year. Some of the friends who I started with or who haven’t stuck with training are still white belts because they refused to consistently invest time into training. I’m a black belt and I teach and compete all over the world. My black belt has opened doors for me in the Jiu-Jitsu world and given me a career. It’s also made me more confident, more intelligent, and most importantly, it’s taught me how to overcome adversity in ways life couldn’t. I’ve also made the best friends I’ve ever had. That’s the icing on the cake. The best time to start Jiu-Jitsu is 10 years ago, the second best time to start is today. Luckily for me, I started 7 years ago. Therapy A lot of men (and women) still stigmatize talk therapy. This is strange to me. I go pretty much every Friday morning when I’m home, and the ideas that come out of therapy are the subject matter for a lot of the stuff you see in my writing. I wish people didn’t stigmatize because therapy can make your life a lot much better. If you think therapy is dumb, it’s probably because you need it and you don’t have the guts to go. To put it bluntly, therapy helps you figure out where you’re fucking up, and you develop strategies so you don’t keep doing that. Therapy is the reason I’m not chasing my ex-girlfriend around and working myself into the ground masochistically anymore. Weight lifting 3x per week Everyone should invest in a gym membership. I only lift weights 3 times per week because most of my exercise is Jiu-Jitsu training, but I still make sure that I lift heavy stuff every week, multiple times per week. Still, 3 times in the weight room every week is better than most people. Dozens of people have written articles about the benefits of lifting weights for your physical health, but I also think having the discipline to get in the weight room and push yourself gives you an incredible mental edge in your life. Plus, just think about how great you’ll look and feel after years upon years of maintaining a gym habit. Quitting gi Jiu-Jitsu (this bugs people, but that sport is a dead-end financially) This investment is really niche and doesn’t apply to most people, but perhaps the concept is valuable. In Jiu-Jitsu, the sport has gi competition (kimono) and no-gi (no kimono). The sport is growing financially on the no-gi side, and it’s stagnating in gi. About a year ago, I decided to quit the gi and focus on no-gi, because I was better at no-gi and there was more money in it. After a year of this, I became ranked in the top 15 in the world and I was able to actually make a living doing Jiu-Jitsu. The lesson here is that you should invest your time wisely. Specialize. If you’re world-class at what you do, the specialist out earns the generalist, every single time. Hopefully, these investments will make you think about more than just where you’re putting your money. Also, you probably shouldn’t take financial advice from random people on Quora ;)

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I get over anxiety?
Answer: This is a mental game that I play to deal with the feeling that everything around me is caving in. It’s called “And then what if _____”… It’s not too fun to play, but it’s really fun to win. “An Idle Mind Is the Devil’s Playground” The moment I get injured and am unable to train Jiu-Jitsu, I realize just how much time I really spend doing Jiu-Jitsu. Between live training, drilling, strength and conditioning, and studying video, I spend probably around 4–6 hours every day immersed in improving myself at Jiu-Jitsu. When you add my teaching responsibilities on top of that, plus all of my writing, it’s honestly a miracle that I have any time to even eat. I hurt my back the other day, and for the moment, I’m stuck on the sidelines. Once you remove the 4–6 hours per day I spend focused on martial arts and knock it down to about .5-1 (I still try to study tape when I’m injured), I am “gifted” with a lot of extra time, and I honestly don’t know how to handle it. I’ll spend some of the extra time writing, but I can only stare at the screen and hammer out words for so long. After I finish writing, I need to do something else, and I honestly don’t know what to do when I’m not training besides sitting and worrying about how I’m getting passed up by my competition. My competition is the best grapplers in the world, so I know that they’re working a lot harder than me when I’m not working at all. Even worse, I don't know how to structure a day that doesn’t involve training. I don’t know how to eat properly when I’m not training. I don’t know what time to get up, what time to go to bed, or how to do anything. Once Jiu-Jitsu is gone, I feel my firm grasp on my reality slipping away. It’s my discipline that keeps me sane, and injuries test my discipline in the most challenging way possible because they remove my favorite part of my discipline routine — my training. Once you take away my training routine, I start to realize that I’m a 24-year-old kid who doesn't really know much of anything about how the world works, and that’s a very scary thing to deal with, especially all by myself, away from my friends and the comfort of the gym. Luckily, I’ve Been Here Before This way of thinking has ruined my day countless times in the past. When I tore my meniscus a few years ago, I had this horrible cycle of depression that lasted for months, and eventually, it led to severe derealization — meaning that my mind was essentially cut off from reality. People often roll their eyes at this, but I promise you that derealization is real, and it’s a hell I wouldn’t wish on my worst enemies. I’ve done some kind of difficult stuff in my life, especially in sports, but without a doubt, winning my battle with derealization is the single toughest victory I have ever pulled off. Doing so gave me mental strength that I didn’t know I had. However, this bout of derealization was triggered by an injury that led to an extended break from Jiu-Jitsu. Because of this, every time I get injured now, I’m “triggered” by memories of the time that I was injured for 6 months and stuck in my head for 9. It’s scary, and I’ve had to create mental strategies that help me continue living, stay peaceful, and even stay happy when I feel like everything is about to fall apart. That’s what takes me to one of my favorite mental games. And Then What If…? My anxiety is kind of like a toddler. No matter what I say to calm its nerves, it always follows up with the same question: “And then what if _____?” (insert some horrible outcome for me) I’ve had some pretty deep internal conversations following this conversation structure, and it’s pretty much how I’ve constructed all of the strategies that I use to deal with my anxiety. It’s similar to Tim Ferriss’s “fear-setting”, but my personal twist is that I take a deeper, more existential approach to managing my fears. I analyze my fears deep down to their core. Doing this has helped me better understand my triggers, my deep-seated hopes, and my darkest fears, and it’s even helped me understand how my own brain chemistry unconsciously dictates the choices that I make. When you can consciously understand the choices that your unconscious mind is making, I believe that you are only a few steps from psychological superpowers. Here’s An Example: Let’s use my current back injury as an example. The first worry that came was “My back is probably going to hurt a bit for the next few weeks”. My anxiety took this thought and ran with it. “And then what if I’m too injured to fight at the ADCC Trials in Poland?”, screams my anxiety, thinking it cares about me and my wellbeing. If that happened, I’d simply keep training and try again at the ADCC Trials in 2024. I’ll probably be even better at Jiu-Jitsu when those come around. “And then what if your back never gets better ever?” screams my anxiety. If that happened, I’d have to accept that my athletic career was over, and then I’d figure out a new way to move forward in my life. I guess I’d become a coach. I might put on 15 pounds. The most famous Jiu-Jitsu coach in the world is so crippled in his, knee, and back that he can barely walk, I’m sure I could be a decent coach with my bad back. I won’t bore you with more of my worries, but the point here is that every time I experience a thought that makes me upset or uncomfortable, I challenge that thought. I use rational thinking to poke holes in irrational thoughts that are fucking up my peace. The result is me being happier and less anxious than I’ve ever been, and it’s pretty damn nice. Hopefully this gives you a new way to think about anxiety :)

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What surprised you the most about living alone?
Answer: Living alone is the bomb diggity — sometimes. I like having “my space”. A workspace. A bedroom. My special chair in the living room. My kitchen is like my special food sanctuary. These things are really nice for me and make me feel safe and secure, but as I’ve gotten older, I’ve found that I’m less married to my routine and more open to accepting others. I love when my girlfriend stays over and I’m sure we’re going to love living together, but even when that occurs I’m going to make it a point to have my own little space. Something that’s “mine”. I'm not sure if this will work in reality, but in theory, it’s what I want. I think that the biggest thing that surprised me about living alone has been all the cleanup. When you have roommates or live with your family, you all (hopefully) share the chores. Someone takes out the trash. Someone does the dishes. Someone cleans the toilet (worst job). When you live alone, all the clean-up is on you. This isn’t a problem unless you’re messy. One of two things will likely happen: You’ll either stop being messy because you don’t want to clean up, or you’ll succumb to your mess and live in filth. If you ever want to get married, I think the first is better. Here’s me, doing the laundry. Cleaning clothes. Livin’ the dream.

Question: What are the best towns to visit in Italy?
Answer: My girlfriend and I spent 3 days in Ravello earlier this year, and it ended up being my favorite place we went to on the whole trip. Here’s the sunrise view from our hotel room on the morning we left. Ravello is known for its views, lemons, and its popular yearly summer music festival. According to the research I did before going on this trip, Ravello is called by some as “la città della musica” — the city of music. But whether you go to the music festival or not, Ravello is a great place to visit. It’s a small town — with a population of around 2500. The food is good (as it is almost everywhere in Italy), the views are stunning, and you’re also kind of… “off the grid”. I loved this. I mostly just hung out with my girlfriend, hung out by the pool, did some journaling, and went on a couple of hikes. I never got bored of the view. Since you’re on the coast, the seafood is a must-try. I forget what this dish was (I don’t speak Italian), but I loved it. In addition to the pasta and the seafood (the pizza is good too), Ravello has a lot of lemons. Well, technically it’s the whole Amalfi Coast that has a lot of lemons, but the lemon craze is really concentrated on “the path of lemons” — which goes from Maiori to Minori and through Ravello. The abundance of lemons means lots of “limoncello”, which is a very popular liqueur, but I’d never had it before going there. I don’t know if any limoncello I have now is going to live up. Here’s a limoncello spritz (a popular limoncello cocktail) that I had with my lady. And here are some funny dick-shaped limoncello bottles we saw at a local shop. Viewer discretion is advised lol. I highly recommend seeing the Amalfi Coast at least once in your life. If for no other reason than to pretend like you’re a character in a Christopher Nolan movie (parts of Tenet were filmed in Positano, another town on the Amalfi Coast that’s WAY more expensive than Ravello). What’s your favorite town to visit in Italy? Next time I’m there, I want to visit Lake Como.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do you think America is the best country in the world?
Answer: I don’t think America is the best country in the world, but I used to. When you grow up in America, you get brainwashed by everyone and their mother with the idea that the “American Dream” is the most special thing ever, that nowhere else in the world is as free as the US, and that the US is the best fucking place on earth. “Oh, and if you don’t agree with that, you can get the fuck out of my damn country.” — patriotic folks, when you express the idea that other countries have freedom too. (According to this website, Singapore is the freest country out there. The US comes in at #25, right behind the UK. I honestly don’t care that we aren’t first, but I don’t love that we act like we are.) America is fucked up, just like everywhere else. However, one thing about America that bugs me is the cultural narcissism that stops us from addressing the flaws that are deeply engrained in our culture. We have problems and we don’t talk about them. We work all the time — much more than in other countries. We are disconnected from our families and each other, and we wear that isolation as a badge of honor that means that we are successful. We also have a serious problem with gun violence, and most people don’t give a shit. We’re disconnected from our families and each other, but we also are disconnected from the tragic events that happen in front of our faces. We see mass shootings on the news all the time. When another shooting happens, people make comments about thoughts and prayers, vow to vote guns away, and then go about their day. They’re not affected because they’re dissociating from the violence as a response to the overwhelming cultural obsession with tragedy and death. We’re obsessed with death, as long as it doesn’t affect us for real. We say that America is the best country in the world, but what actually makes a country great? Is it winning wars? Is it humanitarianism? Is it having nice vacation spots and not being too expensive to travel to? I don’t know what the best country is, but after 2 and a half weeks in Europe, I can’t help but think that the “best country” isn’t the one I’m living in. But the thing is, it’s not about being “the best country”, it’s about being a better country. If you walk around telling everyone you’re the best, there isn’t much incentive to improve. I think that the truth is that Americans, despite their obsession with work and hustle, aren’t any less lazy than the rest of the world. We say that we’re the best so that we don’t have to look our flaws in the face and do the work to improve them. If America was a person, we’d tell them to change. The problem is that changing is hard work.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How do I get rid of jealousy?
Answer: Whenever I feel a pull of jealousy, I ask myself one simple question that stops the spiral: “Would I switch lives, 100%, with the person that I am jealous of?” See, at times, I feel jealous, but the truth is that I’m never really jealous of an entire person. I’m jealous of a moment they’re experiencing. I’m jealous of something they have. 100% of the time, the answer to the question is “no”. I feel jealous sometimes, but I am never so jealous of someone that I would want to switch lives with them 100%. This question is simple, but it helps me stay grounded and realize that I am very blessed. Jealousy is a normal human emotion. Just feeling it does not make you a bad person. The problems arise when you allow jealousy to consume you, which a lot of people do. The question above is my reframe.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is a short, useful, and generally applicable piece of wisdom?
Answer: If your friend only reaches out when they need help, they’re not a good friend. On the flip side, if your friend is there for you when you need help, they’re an extra good friend. You should make sure to be there for them if they ever need help. It’s also okay to give without expecting anything in return — to a point. Eventually, you’re putting yourself in harm's way. Quality friendship is a two-way street. Not all friendships require you to talk daily, but pretty much all friendships require you to be open to connection. If someone is closed off until it’s inconvenient, make room for and invest your energy into better-quality friends. Oh, and if your friend has a cooler beard than you, ask them for beard care tips. Follow their advice.

Question: What keeps you strong, even though you're actually very tired?
Answer: The last thing I wanted to do today was go to the gym. I’ve been dealing with a back injury recently that keeps flaring up, and it’s made me a bit anxious during training, a bit miserable during daily life, and the thought of doing my current least favorite thing (driving with pre-existing back pain) makes me visibly upset. Today, my friends at the gym wanted to train in the gi (the bathrobe things we’re wearing). I hate training in the gi. It’s my least favorite. I like trying to be explosive, scrambly, and athletic during Jiu-Jitsu. Gi training is slower and more technical. For me, it’s less fun right now. However, a few of my friends are getting ready for the World Masters Jiu-Jitsu tournament in a few weeks, so we had to train gi to get them ready. I didn’t want to do it. My back hurts. I’m starting a new diet this week. I’ve got a lot of writing to get done. As grateful as I am for everything, life is stressful right now. I still went to the gym today because I my friends were expecting me there. I still had a good time, didn’t sit out during training, and pushed myself, even though I’m tired. What keeps me strong even when I feel weak is all the people who have similar goals to me. “Family” isn’t the proper term, I guess, but it’s the only one that comes to mind.

Question: How do I deal with haters in my life who want to do harm to me?
Answer: The first thing to do is recognize which type of hater you are dealing with. These are the 5 types of haters: 1. The actual real-life crazy hater. This type of hater is, for the most part, the least dangerous hater that you are going to run into. This hater is not rational. Trolls fall into this category. Sometimes, I get comments and messages from people who don’t have communication skills or common courtesy, but they freaking hate me and everything I stand for. These haters will say ridiculous things to you. They’ll find bizarre ways to talk you down, whether it’s online or in real life. They’ll scour their mind for ways to bring you down. They’ll get creative. You must let it go. These haters suck because they say mean things to your face, but they’ll also probably move on very quickly from you and start hating something else. These people are like wasps. They can be scary, but they’re mostly harmless unless you try to chase them down.  2. The hater who is living vicariously through you. In modern society, there’s this conception that you’re supposed to follow this common path with everyone around you. You’re supposed to go to school, get a job, work like a dog, have kids, raise them, play some golf, vote Republican, and eventually sit back in the nursing home and talk about the “good ole days”, which really weren’t very good at all. After that, it’s over. You die. This path is very common, and it is one of the life paths of least resistance. If you take a different path from this, or any other counter-cultural path, you encounter a lot of adversity. You encounter haters. One of the most common types of haters is someone who follows a life path that sucks the life out of them and becomes spiteful. They cope with their deep unhappiness by hating on and obsessing over someone who is following a path that is different from their own. People have a hard time with those who are different from them, especially when they look happy.  3. The hater who is pretending to be your friend. I’ve lost a lot of friends in the last couple of years. At first, I was losing my “filler” friends in exchange for a life that I created that was full of purpose, adventure, excitement, and all that jazz. Question: What is the better workout, hitting the gym or martial arts?
Answer: In reality, it depends on your goals. For me, the answer is both. If you train martial arts, but don’t have the physical strength to apply your technique in a live situation, your martial arts training is useless. Bruce Lee wasn’t ripped just because he knew how to throw kicks and punches, he also ran constantly and did a crap-ton of push-ups. If you lift or “workout” every day, you’re probably going to have a nice-looking body, but you won’t really learn anything or develop any skills. I love lifting weights, but I love it because lifting weights makes me stronger for martial arts. I love training martial arts, and because of my physical fitness that has been crafted in the gym, I’m strong enough and flexible enough to be able to do almost technique I need. Not everyone can say this. The best workout routine is the one you can stick to that helps you reach your goals.

Question: What is the best mindset to have before going into a relationship?
Answer: I used to go into relationships completely open-minded - ready to experience anything and everything with a new person. Not anymore. I’m just 25 so I can’t call myself old without making everyone roll their eyes at me, but I’m definitely more cynical now. I don’t really want as many new experiences anymore with relationships. I’ve had too many of them. At a certain point, new experiences stop making you interesting and they start making you damaged. If you have too many experiences, you’re eventually very likely to experience some “trauma”. You might not even notice that this is happening until you go to therapy or journal and notice all your unresolved trauma. This makes everything a bit more complicated. That’s why the best mindset to have to go into a relationship is “skeptical optimism”. You must be positive, but you must be vigilant. You must be open to new experiences, but you must know what you want — and almost equally as important — what you don’t want. Pessimism is very unattractive and should be avoided. Doom and gloom makes you a contagion to be around, and not the good kind. That being said, blind optimism — the way I used to be — will make you more susceptible to getting hurt — the way I used to get hurt. You can’t hope to fix people or to be their saving grace. You can just hope to coexist happily with them. If you do enough work on yourself, you’ll realize that this is enough.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What do you consider your strength and why?
Answer: If you asked me a year ago, I would have told you something like “strength is the ability to transcend pain”. My view of strength was all about suffering. I used to think that strength could not exist without pain and suffering. I’ve changed my mind a bit. Today, I think that strength is different. Whether you’re a man, woman, puppy, or goldfish, the foundation of strength does not change. Whether you are lifting weights, overcoming anxiety, or facing adversity in your life, strength is not about pain. Strength is about what you do in the face of life. To me, strength is the ability to endure and transcend the human condition. Strength isn’t about what you’re going through, it’s about what you do. Strength is the ability to do difficult things with a smile. It’s the ability to talk to strangers even though you’re nervous. It’s the ability to be confident when inside you’re more anxious than a puppy on the 4th of July. Strength is the ability to be yourself in a world that would prefer if you’d just shut the fuck up and fit in. “The people's champ must be everything the people can't be.” — Chance the Rapper

Question: How do I find work-life balance?
Answer: This question has been on my radar for a long time, but mostly as a viewer. I didn’t want to answer something I felt I had no idea talking about. That said, I’ve learned a lot about balance this year. This is what most days look like for me—sort of. (It’s not usually this staged but we had to get that content for the IG 😂) For me, it’s really easy to overwork. I’m 25. I’m a competitive grappler, Jiu-Jitsu instructor, and writer. I don’t have kids or a mortgage at the moment. All I do is work and spend time with my friends when I can. The main reason I overwork so much is that I love what I do all day. Everything I do is something I like doing. That sounds corny, but it’s honest. My job is dope. There’s also a deeper reason, but we will get to that in a second. What really bugs me is that sometimes I have to do a little more of it than I’d like. I wish I could have success with less work, but I’ve found that it just doesn’t work like that. For writing, I usually write around 2500-3000 words per day. If I don’t train I usually have the brain power and endurance to get up near 5000. More writing than this usually burns me out, but a lot of pro writers online write way more than I do. For training, I usually do Jiu-Jitsu sparring, technique drilling, and weight training all on the same day. Usually, 3–4 hours per day are spent on physical activity of varying intensity. More training than this usually breaks my body down. Less training impacts my improvement and fitness compared to the other top guys I have to go against in competition. I try to prep all my meals on the weekend so I don’t have to cook during the week, and I make sure to prioritize sleep, stretching, sauna, and taking time to be mindful every day. I also try to keep my social life these days low stress so I don’t feel strung out. I do all the right stuff because if I don’t, I start to feel like my life is falling apart. But here’s the thing. You don’t care about my stupid fucking productivity routine. You don’t care about how often I stretch, how many pages I read per day, or how many words I slam onto the keyboard every day (it’s a lot to all of them). What you care about is how I stay balanced. How I do everything I do without losing my damn mind. I used to struggle a lot with my mental health, primarily because of my lack of balance. It’s not as much of a problem anymore because I’ve figured a few things out about myself. It’s really hard for me to stay balanced because, for the longest time, I thought that my success defined me. I used to prioritize success over everything, and this made me very unhappy. This made me unhappy because though my life was full of excitement and adventure, there was no love in my life. I had no work-life balance because I had no life to look forward to outside of work. Everything I did was work-related because I was scared that if I stopped chasing success, people wouldn’t think I was successful anymore. If they stopped viewing me as successful, I wouldn’t have an identity anymore. My whole life has been very achievement-oriented, and in order to develop balance, I had to realize this and then make active attempts to push back against it. The way that you create “work-life balance” is not by “working” on your balance. If that’s what you’re doing, you’re missing the point. Work-life balance is not something you work at. Most of us don’t need to get better at working, we need to get better at living. You don’t need to work more, you need to live more. You need to laugh more. You need to cry more. You need to think more. You need to align with all the things that make you human. There's something very human about avoiding what makes us human, but that’s what you have to stop doing to have balance in your life. You have to stop trying to be superhuman.
