Question: Does money really buy happiness?
Answer: No, money can’t buy happiness. At least, not lasting happiness. Money can buy you this ice cream pint, and this ice cream pint made me pretty happy for a while, but money can’t buy lasting happiness. Not even lasting money can buy you lasting happiness. To me, lasting happiness comes from a healthy body, a life full of love and adventure, and gratitude for the entirety of the human experience. Happiness is peace. You don’t become happy from doing stuff or buying stuff. Money buys ice cream, not happiness. Ice cream is a metaphor here.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How much does social anxiety interfere with your life?
Answer: For most of my life, I’ve been a bit of a late bloomer. This is primarily because I have a lot of anxiety. It takes me a bit of extra time to get started with things. I hesitate.I’m nervous all the freaking time. I get nervous before competing in martial arts, I get nervous before talking to strangers, and I even get nervous before writing.I I was solo-traveling internationally for the first time ever a few weeks ago, and it scared the living hell out of me. I was in a country where I didn’t speak the language, didn’t know anyone, and I had literally no idea what I’m going to do about it. It was very scary, but it’s also okay. I’ve realized that the truth is that, at the end of the day, the only thing that is really holding me back from having a good experience is the fact that I have anxiety. Everything else is minutiae. Anxiety is the only thing holding me back, and this is what I need to do about it. Scary stuff isn’t always difficult. Last week, I had to cut about 10 pounds in 5 days in order to make weight for my Jiu-Jitsu competition in Poland. I had to fly all the across the world, find and train in gyms that I have never been to before, and then fight against some of the best guys out there. No thanks to the jet lag from flying, I had a really hard time managing my weight for the competition this weekend. It was probably the most challenging weight cut of my life, and I’ve been doing this for a long time. I’ve cut weight hundreds of times, but last weekend, I almost didn’t make it. I was so hungry I couldn’t sleep, so dehydrated that even standing was a challenge, and I was already jet-lagged from the 8-hour time shift between my hometown of Chicago and Poznan, Poland, where the competition was being held.I didn’t eat anything on Thursday or Friday of last week (except for 2 protein bars!), I barely had any water, and I spent a whole hour in the sauna on Friday night. I still had to wake up and run (and spit, which is extra fun) off an entire pound when I woke up on the morning of the competition.I did everything wrong during my first international weight cut, and my body let me know that it was unhappy. I was so miserable that Friday night I was literally wishing that I could get hit by a car so that the weight cut would be ended due to injury. Even after I weighed in successfully, I couldn’t actually eat a meal for nearly 6 hours. I was forced to sip water and the Polish brand of Gatorade and nibble on bananas. This is a physical hell that is common in my sport, but for me, compared to talking to strangers, this was easy for me.I have social anxiety. Welcome to the wacky fuck-space that is my head. Easier, but not better. When I was in the late stages of cutting weight last week, I kept thinking about how terrible what I was doing was for my body.I could feel myself becoming weaker, more dehydrated, and even sicker. But for me, the physical torture is nothing compared to my actual fears. No, I’m not a masochist. I don’t enjoy cutting weight. I don’t enjoy getting beat up. I just would rather cut weight, get beat up, and fight strangers in massive martial arts tournaments than I would go into a bakery in a country where I don’t speak the language. The former is easy. The latter makes me have panic attacks. Asking for directions to the bathroom is a thought that keeps me up at night, while when it comes to fighting in martial arts, I’m as cool as a cucumber. This is a weird problem that I’m dealing with, but dealing with has made me realize that my biggest problem is not what I thought my biggest problem was. Anxiety doesn’t know logic. Anxiety is not a reasonable disorder. It’s not normal. I love the way that we talk about mental health nowadays. It’s inclusive, it’s calming, and it makes me feel more “safe”, but it’s also a bit misleading. The way that people talk about anxiety nowadays completely ignores the fact that experiences with mental health are a spectrum. It tells us that it’s normal to deal with and experience anxiety, but it does not tell us that our experiences with anxiety can be improved or relieved.Inadvertently, the way that we talk about anxiety nowadays is distorted with a defeatist worldview, and the result is that there are a lot of people who are battling anxiety under the impression that there is no way that they can beat anxiety. We feel like dealing with mental health is a losing battle. We’re told to fight our mental health symptoms, but we’re not told that we can win that fight.What if anxiety was your only problem? When I compete in martial arts, I deal with a lot of anxiety still, despite the fact that I appear calm and confident. This is because I do a lot of mental training for competitive situations. My anxiety attempts to protect me by telling me that I don’t have the skills to win. It tells me that I am not tough enough to make weight. It tells me that I’m not strong enough to defeat my opponent. It tells me that my cardio isn’t good enough to last for the entirety of a 9-minute match. Eventually, I’ve to realize that all of these doubts were thoughts in my mind. They were not accurate depictions of reality. My anxiety was painful and uncomfortable, but it was not based on reality. It was based on my insecurities. Anxiety knows that I want to do well in life, so anxiety tells me that I can’t do well in life. Anxiety is a bully in my brain that follows me around and tells me that I’m terrible at everything that I put my mind to. Realizing that is the first step to actually dealing with it. What if we could learn put all of the thoughts aside, and focused only on reality? You can’t always beat your thoughts, but you can ignore them. The anxious thoughts are a bit easier to get rid of during Jiu-Jitsu because I get lost in the “flow” of the activity I enjoy and I am able to push the thoughts away. However, my anxious thoughts do not go away as easily in real life.Whether it’s a first date, a project for a well-paying client, or any other activity that I do that’s important to me, I run the risk of getting stuck in my head and allowing my fears to dictate my experience. Then, I begin to think that my fears are actual depictions of reality, and I get stuck in my real life, as well as in my head.It’s no wonder that I experienced dissociation for 9 months straight — I was stuck in my head, and that allowed me to get stuck in my life. I was disconnected from reality because everywhere I looked both in my life and in my head was a roadblock. To make matters worse, I was beginning to realize that my thoughts were negative, and I stopped trusting them. Everything seemed like a lie, and it distorted my view of reality for quite some time. That’s why I’ve changed the way I look at anxiety. The best natural treatment for anxiety that I have is kind of dumb, but it’s undeniably effective.Before I start to do things, I ask myself “what I would do in the same situation if I had no anxiety?” If I was just living entirely in the moment, how would I behave? What would I say? What would I do?I use my imagination to create a version of myself that exists outside of my anxiety, and I strive to live the life that that version of myself would want me to live. The more that I do what my non-anxious self would want, the happier and more fulfilled I become. Living this way has also opened doors for me both in my personal and professional lives as well because I am no longer unconsciously holding myself back.I used to hold myself back in everything I did. I used to always allow fear to dictate my life, and now, while I am still anxious when I try to order an espresso in an Italian cafe, I am able to feel my fear and do it anyway.That’s pretty cool (and also not that complicated) if you ask me. Ever since I developed some sort of awareness of what mental health is and how it works, I’ve been stunned by the lack of empathy that people have toward those who are literally being attacked by their own minds. However, I also understand the feeling of being frustrated by people who just won’t do anything to improve their situations, even when all of the resources are right in front of them.I know people who have access to therapy, all the books in the world, a loving family, and enough money to buy the most expensive mental health meds, and they still can barely muster the courage to leave the house. I get frustrated when I see this, but I also feel sad, because I know what it’s like to have anxiety hold me back. I’ve been there myself and I’ve seen it in the people closest to me. I know what it’s like to have anxiety be the only thing holding me back.I’m trying to live like the only thing holding me back is a figment of my imagination, because, in some ways, it is.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What can I do to reduce anxiety?
Answer: Anxiety sucks. Here are 5 things I do to make my anxiety suck less. I seek failure. Physical limits are very real, but you really shouldn’t be afraid of them. The fear of failure causes a lot of people a great deal of anxiety. People are scared to lose matches in sports, they’re scared to perform badly at their job, they’re scared to not make enough money, or they’re scared to get rejected by a pretty girl. Failure is everywhere, and on a micro-scale, failure is akin to dying. I used to joke that failure was “dying-lite”. But at the same time, failing makes you realize something very important: Failure makes you realize that failure isn’t so bad. After a while, you’ll realize that in real life, it’s not scary to lose, get rejected, or fail. You recover from pretty much every failure — even the really bad ones. What’s really scary is living in the constant agony that comes when you don’t try to confront your anxiety. Failure is worse in your head than in real life. Seeking failure in endeavors like exercise, dating, or business helps you realize this. I don’t freak out when I break my discipline. I’m not a Navy SEAL. I’m never going to sit here and tell you that in order to succeed you need “unmitigated daily discipline in all things”. I can’t tell you that because I don’t have unmitigated daily discipline myself. Yesterday, for example, I forgot to meditate. The day before, I forgot to read. Saturday last weekend I didn’t write a single damn word. If you saw how much cake I ate on my birthday, you’d probably look at me like I’m insane. However, when it comes to having a good routine, I never give up and I don’t beat myself up for forgetting to do something. Every time I get knocked off the wagon when it comes to reading, meditating, or journaling, I get right back on as soon as I can. While my discipline isn’t perfect, I never stop trying to do the things that are hard for me. I don’t want to wake up early and train and then write all day and teach all night while also squeezing in time to read, study Jiu-Jitsu, and take care of my mind, but I do it anyway. It’s not about never stopping, it’s about never quitting. I’ve found that not doing the hard things is worse than doing them. I’ve also found that beating yourself up for not doing things doesn’t make you want to do them anymore. I don’t care about being the best anymore. I’m a little scared to write this one. In competitive sports, being the best is supposed to be your obsession. You’re supposed to hate losing more than dying and you’re supposed to never accept failure from yourself. You’re supposed to do these things, but I’ll tell you this — that’s an exhausting way to live. Instead of obsessing over who the best is (which is hard because typically “the best” changes depending on a lot of factors), I’m a lot more interested in being the best that I can be. That might sound corny, but this is much more pleasant and actually makes me better in the long run. I have limits. Every time I get a comment from a hater that I should “kill myself” or feel something in my joints snap or pop in a way it’s not supposed to, I’m reminded that I’m not Superman and I can’t do everything. It’s humbling, but my limits are definitely real. Instead of constantly comparing myself to everyone around me, I’m more interested in pushing my own physical and mental limitations for me. In order to have longevity, I’ve needed to drop the constant need for validation to focus on long-term goals. I do something mindful every day. Writing is my job, so a lot of times writing doesn’t make me more mindful. Jiu-Jitsu is also my job, so a lot of times Jiu-Jitsu or working out doesn’t make me more mindful. Having a job that you love is great, but you have to realize that no matter what you do for a living, you need stress relief. You need breaks — probably more than you’re taking. That’s why I take time to do mindfulness every day. I’m not religious about it, but it’s a habit. The problem is, sometimes I get stuck working at the gym for 5 hours in the evening or I get caught up training all day long, and I just don’t have time to sit down, pull out my little cushion, and meditate. If you work a 16-hour day, you’ll understand what I mean. That’s why sometimes, I get my mindfulness through walking. Other times, I get it through driving in silence. If I have time, I like to do the whole “cushion and guided meditation thing”, but what I do isn’t really the point. The point is, every single day, 7 days a week, I take at least a few minutes to be mindful of the world around me and where I am in it. This is the best habit I’ve ever developed for getting out of my head. I call myself out on my BS. From late February to early May of this year, I was constantly dieting and obsessing over my weight for Jiu-Jitsu competitions. I hated it. I hated monitoring my water intake, I hated counting all my calories, and I hated waking up in the middle of the night with a stomach ache from hunger pains. After my last competition where I had to be at my low competition weight, I let myself go a little bit more than normal. I stopped giving a damn about what I ate, how much I ate, and how much salt was on my food. My Yin was extreme rigidity and a religious diet of chicken and broccoli, so my Yang was chocolate chip cookies every night. And? I got kind of chunky. I gained about 8 pounds, give or take, and almost none of it was “good weight”. It was “happy weight”, but definitely not good weight. While there’s nothing wrong with a little “fat and sassy season” (as my mom calls it), I’ve sort of realized over the last few weeks that I am not at my best in terms of being a lean, mean, fighting machine. I don’t feel like I’m as fit as I’ve been earlier this year. For my big competitions this fall, I’m going to really dial in on my nutrition and improve my habits. I’m even working with a nutrition coach for the first time in my career because I know that dieting and weight cutting have always been a challenge for me. This is just one example of how I try to “call myself out on my BS” in my life. Doing this makes me a lot less anxious about anything I am struggling with. I feel like every answer article is the same. Journal. Meditate. See a therapist. Do this. Do that. I get it. At this point, I’ve tried all of it. At this point, I’m kind of tired of the typical anxiety treatments that people describe because I feel like they are devoid of any real insight or value. That’s why for this article, I wanted to focus on concepts instead of habits. You can call yourself out on your BS in a journal, in therapy, or on social media. You can forgive yourself in any area of your life. You can escape competition through authenticity in everything you do. These are concepts, not behaviors. We all have different lives and different habits, but the fundamental concepts that will help you get past anxiety are very similar for all of us. These are the 5 concepts that have worked for me.

Question: Why is it better to train martial arts without a protective cup?
Answer: If you get hit in the dingus in the street, what are you gonna do? Ask the asailant to hold on a second while you recover? You have to be prepared FOR ALL REAL LIFE SCENARIOS. Question: What is the most important thing you have learned about leadership?
Answer: The first “leadership” opportunity I had was helping to run a kid's Jiu-Jitsu program in Chicago. Here are 6 of the most important lessons on leadership that I learned from trying to teach tiny people how to fight. A nice, low-quality photo from belt promotions last fall. Teams are only as strong as their weakest link. Some of my Jiu-Jitsu students are 4. The other day, a girl told me she wasn’t tall enough to lock the bathroom door at the gym. The day before that, a student told me about how proud he was that he weighed 43 pounds. These are tiny humans. It would be pretty easy for me as a teacher to simply disregard these small students and focus more on my bigger, more advanced students. However, this would be bad for the class as a whole because the neglected students would become resentful and disruptive to the learning environment. This is why I try to give energy to all students in the class because everyone is at different levels of skill, competence, and learning aptitude. Yes, I have favorite students. I’m human. I just try to make sure the students can’t tell who my favorites are. Most importantly, I focus on building from the bottom up. If you want respect as a leader, earn it. I’ve won a world championship at purple belt in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Throughout my career, I’ve medaled at major championships 6 times, and I’ve won a bunch of other smaller tournaments as well. I’m not the best competitor of all time by any means, but I have won and accomplished some seemingly impressive things in my time on the mat. However, the truth is that my students (who are 6, remember) really don’t give a crap about me and my medals. They don’t care what belt I am. They don’t care that I go train with world champions whenever I can. They are looking for other qualities that they can respect me for, besides just my prowess as a fighter. Kindness, consistency, and being able to relate to my students are great qualities for any leader start with that do not involve competence of skill. People want to learn from people like them, not people who think they’re above them. Even kids. Especially kids. Silence speaks louder than words. I don’t like to yell. I don’t like being yelled at, so I try to make a conscious effort to never actually “yell” at students in my class. Yelling escalates conflict, and conflict leads to resistance from students. Unless there is a fire in the room or an urgent situation, I don’t really see why negative yelling is good for anyone. Yelling creates apprehension, which leads to resistance. Resistance increases all problems in your situation, and this makes you more likely to have consistent conflict. Sometimes, I will yell “good job!”, because I noticed my coach doing that growing up and I found it really encouraging. Positive reinforcement at a high volume is good. Negative criticism (for lack of a better term) should be brought on gently. When there is conflict in my class, I find that silence is better for finding solutions and deescalating the situation. If there was a serious problem in the class, like a fire, panicking would only make it worse. Why would it be okay to panic over comparatively small problems, like minor misbehavior? Your team can sense your fatigue. People around you can tell when you’re tired, and they can tell when you are slacking off. They can also tell when you’re fighting your fatigue resiliently. The second sentence is more important than the first one. Some days, when I come into teach, I’ve already trained twice that day, worked, had phone calls, taught private lessons, or wrote. On rare occasions, I’ve already done all of the above by the time it’s time to teach my kiddos how to do armbars. People can sense when I’m allowing this fatigue to get to me. On the days that I’m too tired and “a little out of it”, the kids are out of it too. As a leader or teacher of any type, you have to keep it together. People can sense when you’re off, and their behavior will reflect the energy you put into their development. Grit is a contagion. It is not taught. My Jiu-Jitsu coach, Jeff, is one of the grittiest individuals I have ever met. Grit, by definition, is the combination of “passion and perseverance” that allows someone to stick with a given activity for a very long time. Jeff has over 25 years of MMA and Jiu-Jitsu experience. At his first MMA fight (which took place when I was an infant), there were no weigh-ins and gloves were optional. Point is, he’s a tough dude, not to mention a really smart guy and a fantastic coach. However, right now I’m focused on his grit. If I sit there and tell people to be tough, it doesn’t really inspire them to be tougher themselves. It ends up looking silly, hypocritical, and unhelpful for the entire room. Jeff doesn’t tell his students to be tough — ever. He just is tough, and that is what inspired me to become someone who can persist through injuries, compete under pressure, and keep putting myself out there no matter what. This is what I strive to create in my students, through leading by example. You must learn to see the individuals in the group. Your team only exists because you have decided that it does. Think about that for a second. Teams are socially constructed. The Chicago Bulls are different from the Los Angeles Lakers because we have decided that they are. As a coach, teacher, or leader, you have to learn to relate to people both individually and as a group. People need to feel seen when they work with a team. If you spend too much time focusing on the team and not enough time on the individuals, people will stop learning, start acting out, and become unhappy. Love makes people work together. Give people on your team a little bit of love. Unless you’re running an empire in the 1500s, it’s better to be loved than feared.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Can you lose your black belt in martial arts?
Answer: Ugh yes. This is the worst. Sometimes, I leave it at the gym. Other times, it’s hidden under a blanket in my apartment. Once I left it at a hotel I stayed at when I was traveling for a competition. I lost that one for good. Can the black belt be taken away from you? Not… really… The belt is a concept. Even if someone says “you are no longer a black belt in my eyes”, they still cannot take away the fact that you earned your black belt. The belt is a measure of skill and a reflection of the time and effort that you have put into training. It’s also not really the point of training. Even if you commit a horrible crime or something like that, you wouldn’t lose your black belt. You’d just be a shitty human who also has a black belt in martial arts. Black belts aren’t magic. They’re mostly just to hold your jacket together and keep your pants up. Everything else is semantics.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why is everyone in their 20s so confused?
Answer: In Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, there are 5 belts. Generally, it takes about 2 years at each belt (sometimes more) to eventually progress to your black belt. It takes a while to learn Jiu-Jitsu. When you’re a white belt, you don’t know anything. When you’re a blue belt, you think you know stuff, but you know way less than you think you do. Purple belt, you know a little more. Brown belt, you think you’re close to mastery. Then, you get your black belt and you realize that the only thing you know is how little you know. Likewise, life takes a while to learn about. Say you live to 100ish because you’re healthy and have good genetics or whatever. You’re going to spend 20 years at each belt of life. But realistically, most people don’t live to be 100. Similarly, most people who start Jiu-Jitsu don’t ever get their black belts. If you want to get your black belt in life, there’s really nothing to do but put in the time. To live. To experience everything day by day. If you’re in your 20s, you’re probably a blue belt. That means you’ve got the fundamentals down, but you’re still pretty clueless. You’re confused because you’re probably realizing that knowing the fundamentals alone doesn’t get you to a high level. You don’t know as much as you think. I am writing this as someone in their 20s. If there’s I’ve learned in the last few years it’s that I don’t know as much as I think I know. I wouldn’t call myself confused, but who knows what I think of my present self in 10, 20, or even 50 years from now. I’m a little nervous to find out. Maybe Quora will still be around and I’ll visit this answer to see how much I’ve learned compared to how much I thought I knew. “You must understand the whole of life, not just one little part of it. That is why you must read, that is why you must look at the skies, that is why you must sing, and dance, and write poems, and suffer, and understand, for all that is life.” ― Jiddu Krishnamurti

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What's wrong with the fitness industry?
Answer: The fitness industry is completely disconnected from “health”. Here’s a photo of me from a few years ago, probably the leanest I’ve ever been. Sorry for the douchey picture… trying to make a point here 😂. All I did during this 6-month period of my life was work out, eat cleaner than a nun’s vocabulary, and listen to personal development podcasts. I was miserable. Life sucked. All I have from that period looking back are a few pictures of me with a nice 6 pack. I’ve always done combat sports (first wrestling, now Jiu-Jitsu), so I’ve always paid attention to my weight so that I can make weight for competitions, but I never really paid attention to aesthetics. However, there’s this myth in the fitness world that being fitter will solve all of your problems, and I drank the kool-aid. You might be a bad person, you might have terrible social skills, and you might be broke, but you if you have a 6 pack, people will be jealous of you. That’s kinda fucked up, isn’t it? Nonetheless, one summer, I decided that if I got leaner, girls would like me more. I’d be more successful if I had the body of someone who was more successful. And so, I committed to the gym harder than I ever had before. The irony is that I never had time to date anyone or work on any true personal development because I was always in the gym, either training Jiu-Jitsu or lifting weights or running or biking. I was working out for 3–6 hours per day, 6–7 days per week. My fitness was my obsession. Ultimately, this made me a worse athlete and an unhappier person. A few months after I got super duper lean, I had a bad injury, was sidelined for 6 months, and I chubbed right back up. I was more depressed than I’d ever been. That was when I experienced that episode of derealization I’ve written about a few times before. Health and fitness aren’t always the same thing. Learn to become healthy. Then you can think about fitness. The fitness industry uses extreme examples of health and fitness to sell products to you. I got really lean by working out all day long, eating great, and prioritizing my fitness over everything else. I lived an extreme lifestyle. However, health does not come from extremes. In sports, this is especially true. Optimal performance in sport does not come from zero percent body fat (in that photo, I’m probably between 10–15% body fat). Optimal performance comes from comfort. We obsess about getting out of our comfort zones, but that’s not what it’s really about. You’re not supposed to live your life in discomfort, you’re supposed to expand the area of your comfort zone so that fewer situations make you uncomfortable. If you’re struggling with insecurities about your body, hiding away by yourself doing crunches and slamming protein shakes is the antithesis of your problem. EDIT: Here’s what I look like now. This pic is a few months old, but I don’t take a ton of shirtless pics anymore because I realized I was only doing it before as a vanity metric. This is kinda the best I got 😂 This pic is a good one because it was during the off-season when I wasn’t cutting weight for a competition. In the pic below I weigh about 20 pounds more than the pic above. I’m happier. I’m also stronger in every single major lift. I could also beat the child in the pic above’s ass 😂 The point is that optimal performance body and optimal aesthetics body aren’t always the same.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What made you resign from your previous job?
Answer: For the last year and a half or so, I’ve been working as a social media manager for 6–12 businesses. This was my “regular job” while I was pursuing my passions of writing and Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Last week, I said “fuck it”, and quit. Here’s why: Every time I’ve worked for someone else, the working relationship has gone up in flames. As a kid, I hated being told what to do. I hated school. I hated bosses. I’m an athlete, and for years I even had a problem taking advice from coaches and listening during technical instruction during wrestling practice. I used to make myself throw up when I was a baby just because it pissed my mom off. My amazing mother is a trooper to put up with my bullshit. Maybe I’m a demon. Maybe, I just need to march to the beat of my own drummer. My problem with authority was the leading contributing factor to my lack of success in my school years and early adulthood. I always wanted to do my own thing, and I was never allowed to. I always had to sit back and listen. I always had to follow orders. But not anymore. Now, I’m free. This is the process that I used to get to a point where I can quit my job and go all-in on my dreams of writing, teaching, and grappling: Honestly, you might not love where this answer is going… There wasn’t a secret to me becoming a “full-time writer” and a professional athlete. I didn’t discover a secret platform, create a secret product or course, or take a bunch of steroids. If anything, I mostly failed on my way here. I still fail every day. Recently, I actually wrote an e-book that hardly anyone bought. I spent most of the last fall being so injured that I couldn’t grapple or lift weights. I lost a lot of matches last year. On my year and a half-long journey to a career that I actually wanted to have, I mostly messed things up. Most of my articles received under 100 views. My first 89 Quora answers were viewed less than 6000 times, while my ensuing answers have been viewed several millions of times. All I’ve done has been practice every day, work really hard, study my game, and get a little bit lucky. That’s fuckin’ it. Now, I’m able to take the next step. I wish I could tell you there was more to it. I burned myself out, built myself back up, and then did it all over again time and time again. I’ve written and trained just about every single day for several years now for this freedom, and the “prize” that I was given was the opportunity to go “all-in” on the dream life that I designed when I was 19-years-old and living in my college dorm room. I wrote until they had to give me a job. My success on Medium/Quora during the fall gave me some higher-paying writing jobs that made my life a lot more comfortable. I did the math, and my newly acquired ghostwriting gigs would end up paying me more than double what I was being paid to write social media content previously. This made me realize that my previous employers were taking advantage of my skills and work ethic, and I felt compelled to make an escape. I felt cheated, angry, and manipulated, and this frustration gave me a chip on my shoulder that fueled some of the best writing that I believe I’ve ever put out. It was hard work. It was also dumb luck. I won’t lie to you. But at the end of the day, the most important factor to building my career online was writing was doing so much damn stuff that it was literally impossible for me to be ignored. I’ve written more than 250 articles on Medium. I’ve published more than 100 newsletters. I’ve written hundreds of Quora answers and posted a butt-ton of articles on LinkedIn and Twitter. I’ve had hundreds of grappling matches. I’ve done this stuff for so freaking long. So freaking long. I put my name out there so much that some people who were looking for a ghostwriter thought that they would give me a shot, and so far, that shot is working out. Then, I leveraged my skills close to home. Jiu-Jitsu is my first love. I train every day, I teach nearly every day, and I travel the US and beyond training and competing in various competitions. Writing and teaching give me the freedom to live the life I want, and all of my non-Jiu-Jitsu and writing clients were holding me back from the opportunities that would give me even more freedom. I also got my first real sponsor for Jiu-Jitsu this year, the guy in the picture at the top of this article. I’m lucky that I have a sponsor, but I also worked my butt off for years and years (mid-April marks 7 years of Jiu-Jitsu and 12 years of grappling for me) in order to become an athlete who was worth sponsoring. Then, I got to combine writing with Jiu-Jitsu when I was asked to start writing his company’s bi-monthly blog. It was a dream come true. Now, I’m writing articles on martial arts, ghostwriting articles, running my own blog, building my writing business, and teaching Jiu-Jitsu classes, lessons, and seminars. All of this added up to me not only not needing my previous freelance gigs, but I actually didn’t have time to do their work anymore. I had to quit these jobs so that I could focus on quality over quantity. I had to quit so that I could make my life manageable. I had to quit so that my future work would work. And so, just last week, I said “screw it”, and I did it. Now, there’s no going back. I hate being that guy who tells people “if you want what I want, you have to work for it”, but I honestly can’t tell you how else I’ve gotten to where I am. I don’t think I’m super talented, I do think I got pretty lucky, and I also worked my ass off for the life that I have created. I’ve practiced nearly every day for several hours per day for a decade for a chance to chase the life of my dreams. Only time will tell if I’m able to sustain this momentum. The story is far from over.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the best life advice you would give?
Answer: Let’s talk about pleasure and how it relates to a good life. My whole life, I was taught to demonize things that felt good. Early on, this way of thinking was helpful. It made me stop eating so much junk food. It made me stop flooding my brain with porn. It made me stop chasing people who were bad for me. But over time, I started to get depressed from all of the self-inflicted constraints that I put on my own life. I removed all of the immediate pleasure from my life in the name of self-development, and I fucking hated it. People seem to think that there is an inverse relationship between success and pleasure, but is this really true? I think it’s partially true. Our ideas of pleasure are also heavily influenced by religion, past experiences, and stuff we see online. Honestly, today I’m just fed up with all the self-help bullshit I see from startup bros on Twitter that tells me that I have to take cold showers, wake up at 4 am, and chant positive affirmations into the mirror like the characters in Candyman chant for Candyman to appear. You can’t make your life better by just saying positive shit to yourself. You have to talk nicely to yourself, and then you have to go out and do nice things for yourself. A better life doesn’t come from waking up at 4 am every day or optimizing your optimized morning routine for the 42nd time, it comes from having the discipline to weather any storm you go through. Discipline is tough to sell, so people give it fancy packaging. The measure of discipline is not through how you spend the The real test of discipline is not the ability to abstain from pleasure or things that feel good. It’s pretty easy to abstain from things once you get in the habit of abstaining from them. The real test of discipline is the ability to do things that feel good every once and a while without over-indulging to the point of excess. Try to eat one Oreo. Try and take one day off work. Can you do it? For me, it’s hard. It’s easier to just burn myself into the ground. I’ve been on both ends of the spectrum, and for me, discipline to the point of excess is not a whole lot better for happiness than eating pizza to excess. You’ll just dig your own grave in a different part of the cemetery. The best life advice that I would give is to strive to be reasonably disciplined in your life. You don't need to take cold showers. You don't need to do intermittent fasting. You don't need to wake up at 4 in the morning. You don't need to do what the self-help Twitter guy tells you to do. You need to be disciplined, not drastic. Drastic behavior is a sign of projection. The second best piece of life advice that I would give is to never sit on social media and tell people to take cold showers and wake up earlier.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are 10 or fewer good habits for a 24 year old that can make life better?
Answer: I’m 24, about to be 25 in August. These are 10 habits that I’ve used to become a quick learner and a happier person. Maybe they can help you too. First, let me provide a little context on how I discovered these habits and their effectiveness for me and my growth. In November of 2021, I competed in and lost in the second round of the ADCC Trials (a qualifier for the most important submission grappling tournament in the world) in a division that had more than 150 athletes. At the time, this was the largest submission grappling tournament I had ever competed in, and I had a piss-poor performance. In April of 2022 (5 months later), I competed in the second iteration of the Trials which was far more competitive, and I took 4th place in a division that had more than 250 athletes. I came in unseeded, and I upset 3 of the top 16 seeds in the tournament. Most people saw my results and wondered, “Who is this guy and where did he come from?” I wasn’t surprised though, this was something I’d obsessed over for the 5 months in between competitions. I completely changed as an athlete in 5 months. Essentially, these are the 10 most important habits that allowed me to go from losing in the second round to placing 4th at the biggest grappling tournament in North America in just 6 months. Who knows what will happen when I try again for ADCC in 2 years. 1. Study the people you wish to be like one day. I’m obsessed with analyzing the behavior patterns of world-class athletes and writers. In time, this study makes my imitation of their behavior second nature. The longer you act like a world-class performer, the sooner you will become one. 2. Seek failure every single day. You should not push your physical limits every day, but you should fail every day. Learning to fail develops a resiliency to failure, and this resiliency makes you unbreakable. When you’ve lost every single day, you begin to understand that failure is not merely an indication of inadequacy. This frees you from the anxiety of failure and allows you to maximize your preparation and performance. 3. Specialize. In Jiu-Jitsu, there are 2 “forms” that are practiced. There is gi Jiu-Jitsu (where kimono is worn) and no-gi Jiu-Jitsu, where simple athletic wear is worn in place of the kimono. After losing in the first round of my first run at the ADCC Trials, I chose to quit training in the gi. This was met with some resistance from people close to me, but nonetheless, I specialized. This specialization took my focus and discipline to the next level. “You can be anything, but you can’t be everything.” — David Allen 4. Micro-drilling. I swear by micro-drilling in everything that I do. Micro-drilling is the habit of practicing the same activity over and over again, in complete isolation. This is a drill for drilling muscle memory in your head at a low impact, meaning that there is a low risk of burnout or injury. This will train your body and mind to instantly provide the proper reaction to the proper situation. This will take your technique (in any activity) from good to great. In sports, this makes a world of difference. In writing, the main micro-drills I use are headline writing, tweet writing, and poetry writing. 5. Mindfulness. This isn’t sexy, but getting tangible results at a world-class level rarely is. Anxiety is what destroys potential. World-class athletes lose to anxiety before they even step out to compete. Many aspiring writers never publish anything because they are too anxious about the impending results. By leaving your head, you realize all of the limiting beliefs that are holding you back. I do this through mental training and meditation. 6. Visualization. Most people don’t visualize and it shows. By now, I can always tell which competitors are visualizing their performances and which are competing just to see how they do. Those who visualize important moments act at the moment as if they have been there before. The moment is not too big for them. When the moment is not too big for you and you can function under pressure the way you do in practice, all of your isolated training and hard work is able to come to fruition. 7. Dropping my sob story. Writing is my outlet for my emotions, my anxiety, and anything else that makes me upset. I need this outlet to live a full and happy life in reality. I get everything I need to get out of my head through writing, and because of that, I’m able to go through (most of) my life without my head being full of the thoughts that hold me back from realizing my potential. If I sound whiny on the internet, it’s because I’m trying to not be whiny in real life. When the “sob story” narrative is removed from my head, I’m able to channel the mind of a “winner” who can handle adversity more efficiently than I would have ever thought possible. 8. Sacrifice. Yes. I have a habit of sacrifice. Pretty much every weekend in between the 2 ADCC Trials, I sacrificed “going out” and partying or eating unhealthily because I wanted to prove that I had the ability to perform at the highest levels of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. For the last 6 weeks of my training camp, my diet was nearly perfect. I sacrificed the possibility of getting into a serious relationship in the name of this goal because it wouldn't be fair to my potential partner. I sacrificed money and time to focus on my goal. I even quit my job. This was a temporary period of my life where intense sacrifices were required for rapid progress. 9. Chasing down the people who I wanted to learn from and be like. A few months before I went to my second attempt at the ADCC Trials, I went on a training trip to Austin, Texas, where I trained with some of the top no-gi grapplers in the world today. I also took a class from John Danaher, who is widely considered to be the best Jiu-Jitsu coach in the world today. This weekend trip made me look at my sport through a more professional lens. It was also motivating and incredibly inspiring for my work ethic to surround myself with coaches like that. It made me want to go home and work in a way that would impress them. 10. Proper nutrition, sleep, and hydration. Whether you are trying to be a world-class athlete or a world-class writer or a world-class underwater basketweaver, you must master the art of optimal physical health. Part of the reason that I had such a poor performance on my first attempt at the ADCC Trials was that I had been battling back and rib injuries for the months prior. In the second attempt, I was in good physical health, had a good weight cut, and was mentally dialed in. This made all the difference. For more articles and essays like this one, check out my newsletter below.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: How long would it take to become a black belt in Brazilian jiu-jitsu?
Answer: I got my black belt in 7 years. Here’s me, on the day I got my black belt: I trained nearly every day to get my black belt for almost exactly 7 years. I think I got my black belt about a week or so after my 7 anniversary of training. I had a few breaks because of injuries, but for the most part, I trained through and around my injuries. The longest I’ve gone without training since I started in 2015 was about 3 weeks, after I had meniscus surgery in 2018. I was training and competing about as close to full-time as it can get, and I got my black belt in 7 years. The average hobbyist will get their black belt in about 8–10 years, if they stay consistent. There are stories about guys like former UFC champion BJ Penn, who got his black belt in just 3 years. You don’t see these stories much anymore because in the 2010s that set in place time limit requirements for each belt. In 2022, the fastest you can get your black belt in BJJ while following these requirements is 4.5 years (2 years at blue, 1.5 at purple, 1 at brown), but that assumes that you spent zero days as a white belt. I spent 13 months as a white belt, 2 years as a blue belt, 2 years and 3 months as a purple belt, and 1 year and 8 months as a brown belt. I don’t usually plug products, but I’ll leave this link here because this product is free. Here’s a short ebook I wrote a year ago on ways that you can learn Jiu-Jitsu faster. They helped me go from complete beginner to world champ in just 4 years.
